vjimc-2014-cat2-01.title: Cauchy's mean value theorem with $e^{x^2/2}$
vjimc-2014-cat2-01.body:
Let $\varepsilon>0$ and choose $x_0>0$ with $\left|f(x)+\frac{f'(x)}x\right|<\frac\varepsilon2$ for $x\ge x_0$. Let $g(x)=e^{x^2/2}f(x)$ and $h(x)=e^{x^2/2}$. Then
$$g'(x)=xe^{x^2/2}\left(f(x)+\frac{f'(x)}{x}\right),\qquad h'(x)=xe^{x^2/2}>0 .$$
For $x>x_0$, Cauchy's mean value theorem on $[x_0,x]$ gives $\eta\in(x_0,x)$ with
$$\frac{g(x)-g(x_0)}{h(x)-h(x_0)}=\frac{g'(\eta)}{h'(\eta)}=f(\eta)+\frac{f'(\eta)}{\eta}.$$
Dividing numerator and denominator by $e^{x^2/2}$ and writing $\delta(x)=e^{(x_0^2-x^2)/2}\in(0,1)$:
$$f(x)-f(x_0)\delta(x)=\left(f(\eta)+\frac{f'(\eta)}\eta\right)\big(1-\delta(x)\big).$$
Hence
$$|f(x)|\le|f(x_0)|\,\delta(x)+\frac\varepsilon2 .$$
Since $\delta(x)\to0$ as $x\to\infty$, there is $\tilde x\ge x_0$ with $|f(x_0)|\delta(x)<\frac\varepsilon2$ for $x\ge\tilde x$, and then $|f(x)|<\varepsilon$. As $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary, $f(x)\to0$. ∎

vjimc-2014-cat2-01.title: Integrating factor
vjimc-2014-cat2-01.body:
Let $\varphi(x)=f(x)+\frac{f'(x)}{x}\to0$, so $\left(e^{x^2/2}f(x)\right)'=x e^{x^2/2}\varphi(x)$. Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and $x_0>0$ with $|\varphi|<\frac\varepsilon2$ on $[x_0,\infty)$. (We compare monotone functions instead of integrating $\varphi$, which need not be integrable.) The function $G(t)=e^{t^2/2}\big(f(t)-\frac\varepsilon2\big)$ has $G'(t)=te^{t^2/2}\big(\varphi(t)-\frac\varepsilon2\big)<0$ on $[x_0,\infty)$, so $G$ is decreasing and for $x>x_0$
$$e^{x^2/2}\Big(f(x)-\frac\varepsilon2\Big)\le e^{x_0^2/2}\Big(f(x_0)-\frac\varepsilon2\Big),\quad\text{i.e.}\quad f(x)\le\frac\varepsilon2+\Big(f(x_0)-\frac\varepsilon2\Big)e^{(x_0^2-x^2)/2}.$$
The same argument with $\tilde G(t)=e^{t^2/2}\big(f(t)+\frac\varepsilon2\big)$ (increasing, as $\varphi>-\frac\varepsilon2$) gives $f(x)\ge-\frac\varepsilon2+\big(f(x_0)+\frac\varepsilon2\big)e^{(x_0^2-x^2)/2}$. Letting $x\to\infty$, $\limsup|f(x)|\le\frac\varepsilon2$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $f(x)\to0$. ∎

vjimc-2014-cat2-02.title: A primitive sixth root of unity
vjimc-2014-cat2-02.body:
Since $6\mid|A|$ and $|A|\mid p-1$, we have $p\ge7$, so $p$ is odd. Every finite subgroup of the multiplicative group of a field is cyclic, so $A$ is cyclic and contains an element $a$ of order $6$.

Then $a^6=1$ and $a^3\ne1$, so $(a^3-1)(a^3+1)=0$ gives $a^3=-1$. Factor $0=a^3+1=(a+1)(a^2-a+1)$. Since $a$ has order $6$, $a\ne-1$ (which has order $2$), so
$$a^2-a+1=0,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad a^2+1=a .$$
Thus $x=a^2$, $y=1$, $z=a$ are elements of $A$ (note $1\in A$, being a subgroup) with $x+y=z$. ∎

(Alternatively: since $a^2\ne1$, $a+a^3+a^5=a\,\frac{1-a^6}{1-a^2}=0$, hence $a+a^5=-a^3=1$, and $x=a$, $y=a^5$, $z=1$ also work.)

vjimc-2014-cat2-03.title: Generating functions
vjimc-2014-cat2-03.body:
Work with formal power series. For $N\ge1$,
$$(1+x)^{-N}=\sum_{m\ge0}(-1)^m\binom{N+m-1}{N-1}x^m$$
(the negative binomial series; e.g. by induction on $N$ using $\sum_{i\le m}\binom{N+i-1}{N-1}=\binom{N+m}{N}$).

Now use the identity
$$(1-x)^{k+2}=(1-x^2)^{k+2}\,(1+x)^{-(k+2)} .$$
**Left side:** the coefficient of $x^k$ is $(-1)^k\binom{k+2}{k}=\binom{k+2}{2}=\frac{(k+1)(k+2)}2$, as $k$ is even.

**Right side:** $(1-x^2)^{k+2}=\sum_n(-1)^n\binom{k+2}nx^{2n}$, so the coefficient of $x^k$ is
$$\sum_{n=0}^{k/2}(-1)^n\binom{k+2}{n}\cdot(-1)^{k-2n}\binom{(k+2)+(k-2n)-1}{k+1}=\sum_{n=0}^{k/2}(-1)^n\binom{k+2}{n}\binom{2(k-n)+1}{k+1},$$
using that $k-2n$ is even. Comparing the two coefficients proves the identity. (Check $k=2$: $\binom53-4\binom33=10-4=6=\frac{3\cdot4}2$.) ∎

vjimc-2014-cat2-04.title: Laplace-transform representation of the logarithm
vjimc-2014-cat2-04.body:
**Lemma (Frullani).** For $s>0$: $\displaystyle\ln s=\int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-t}-e^{-st}}{t}\,dt$.

*Proof.* $\frac{e^{-t}-e^{-st}}t=\int_1^se^{-ut}\,du$. For $s\ge1$ the integrand $e^{-ut}$ is positive, so by Tonelli
$$\int_0^\infty\!\!\int_1^se^{-ut}\,du\,dt=\int_1^s\!\!\int_0^\infty e^{-ut}\,dt\,du=\int_1^s\frac{du}u=\ln s;$$
for $s<1$ the same computation applies to $-\int_s^1$. $\square$

**Fubini is allowed.** Let $\|f\|=\max|f|$ and $K(s,t)=\frac{e^{-t}-e^{-st}}{t}$. For $s=x+y\in[2a,2b]$: if $0<t\le1$, $|K|\le|s-1|\le 2b+1$ (mean value theorem, since $|\frac{d}{du}e^{-ut}|\le t$); if $t\ge1$, $|K|\le e^{-t}+e^{-2at}$. So $|f(x)f(y)K(x+y,t)|$ is bounded by $\|f\|^2$ times an integrable function of $t$, uniformly in $(x,y)\in[a,b]^2$, and we may integrate in any order.

**Computation.** Let $F(t)=\int_a^bf(x)e^{-xt}\,dx$. Then
$$\iint f(x)f(y)\ln(x+y)\,dx\,dy=\int_0^\infty\frac1t\left[e^{-t}\Big(\int_a^bf\Big)^2-\iint f(x)f(y)e^{-xt}e^{-yt}\,dx\,dy\right]dt=-\int_0^\infty\frac{F(t)^2}{t}\,dt,$$
because $\int_a^bf=0$ and $\iint f(x)f(y)e^{-(x+y)t}\,dx\,dy=F(t)^2$. (The last integral converges: it equals the left side, and also directly $|F(t)|=\left|\int f(x)(e^{-xt}-1)\,dx\right|\le\|f\|(b-a)bt$ near $0$ and $|F(t)|\le\|f\|(b-a)e^{-at}$.) Since $F(t)^2/t\ge0$,
$$\int_a^b\!\!\int_a^bf(x)f(y)\ln(x+y)\,dx\,dy=-\int_0^\infty\frac{F(t)^2}{t}\,dt\le0 .$$
∎
